items.prompt: What is a time series?
choices: Values recorded at regular intervals, in order
Any pile of numbers with no particular order
One measurement taken at a single moment in time
items.explanation: Regular spacing and order are what make it a series.

items.prompt: Why does order matter in a time series?
choices: Order only changes how the chart is coloured
It never matters, because only the average counts
Shuffling it destroys the direction over time
items.explanation: The shape over time is the information; the average alone hides it.

items.prompt: What does "trend" mean?
choices: A single unusual value
The direction values are really moving
The average of all values
items.explanation: Trend is the underlying direction once wiggles are set aside.

items.prompt: What is noise in a series?
choices: Fluctuation that is not a change of course
The slope of the line fitted to every point
The forecast we make for next month's value
items.explanation: Noise is movement that does not reflect a lasting shift.

items.prompt: Bills went $52 then $80. How big is the jump?
Why can two points not reveal noise?
choices: Two points are always completely random noise
Any two points make a perfect line
A line needs at least three points to exist
items.explanation: A line fits two points exactly, so nothing looks off.

items.prompt: What is extrapolation?
choices: Forecasting past the data by continuing a trend
Averaging the data into a smaller set of groups
Deleting unusual points from the series entirely
items.explanation: It means extending a pattern beyond the observed range.

items.prompt: The quick forecast of $248 used how many of the six bills?
choices: Four
Six
Two
items.explanation: It used only month 5 and month 6.

items.prompt: A friend says "the trend is $28 a month" from the jump $52 to $80. What is the strongest objection?
choices: The jump should have been measured in percent, not in dollars
Two points cannot separate a real change from one odd month
Six months of data is too short to compute any difference
The bill should be averaged over only the latest month
items.explanation: A single difference is one observation. The earlier five months show a flat pattern the jump has not yet earned the right to overrule.
items.reference:
What two points can and cannot tell you
two points: always a perfect straight line
six points: a line that can miss by a lot
the $80 bill: new direction or one hot month?
need more history to separate trend from noise
Why: any two points fit a line exactly, so only more points can reveal whether a jump is direction or noise.
items.learnMore:
Trend versus noise

A forecast built from the last jump treats that jump as the whole trend. Reading all the points lets you see how far the jump sits from the earlier pattern, and the sensible next move is to ask what caused it.

Common mistake

Computing a rate from the two latest values and calling it the trend. The rate may be pure noise, and two points cannot show which.
items.reflection: Think of a number you track in daily life, such as a commute time or a grocery bill. Which recent change did you treat as a new normal, and what would you have needed to see to be sure?

items.prompt: Which extra fact would best help decide whether month 6 was noise or a new direction?
choices: The exact date the provider printed the month-6 bill
Whether month 6 had thirty days or thirty-one
Whether the cause of the jump is still present in later months
The average bill in a neighbouring building
items.explanation: Persistence is the test: a one-off cause fades and a lasting change stays in later values.

items.prompt: Weeks 1-10 climb about 2 signups a week, then weeks 11-12 read 80 and 120. Which statement is justified?
choices: The true growth is 40 a week, because it is the latest change we have seen in the data
The true growth is 2 a week, because the early weeks are always exact
No growth rate can ever be known, because every series contains at least some noise
One 40-a-week jump is a single observation; ten weeks support the 2-a-week climb
items.explanation: Ten points agree on a gentle slope. Two points disagree sharply, which is worth investigating but does not erase the rest.

items.prompt: What is the 3-week moving average of 30, 33 and 36?
What does a moving average do to a single spike?
choices: Spreads it across several results, softening it
Removes it completely from the series
Makes it twice as large as before
items.explanation: The spike stays in the window for several steps but is divided by the window size.

items.prompt: The week-12 3-week moving average of 50, 80 and 120 is?
What does a larger window do?
choices: Rougher and quicker to react to changes
Smoother but slower to react
Identical to the raw data, unchanged
items.explanation: More values in each average damp wiggles and delay response.

items.prompt: A window of 3 averages which values?
choices: The current value and the two before it
Only the current value, nothing else
Three values chosen at random from the series
items.explanation: A moving window slides along the series one step at a time.

items.prompt: Why does a moving average lag behind a sudden jump?
choices: It ignores the newest value
It sorts the values before averaging
Older values are still in the window
items.explanation: The newest value is only one third of the average.

items.prompt: What is a moving average mostly used for?
choices: Predicting the exact next value
Seeing direction through week-to-week wiggle
Counting how many weeks passed
items.explanation: It is a smoother, not a forecaster.

items.prompt: What does a window of 1 give?
choices: The raw data unchanged
A flat line at the overall average
Always zero
items.explanation: Averaging one value returns that value.

items.prompt: Weeks 10-12 read 50, 80 and 120, yet the 3-week moving average at week 12 is only 83.3. What explains the gap?
choices: The average discards the largest value in each window it covers
Moving averages always cut the newest value by exactly one third
The week-12 spike was removed as an outlier before the averaging
The window still holds 50 and 80, which hold the average back
items.explanation: The newest value counts for one third, so earlier values drag the result toward them. This is the lag.
items.reference:
3-week moving average of the signups
week 9: (44 + 42 + 47) / 3 = 44.3
week 10: (42 + 47 + 50) / 3 = 46.3
week 11: (47 + 50 + 80) / 3 = 59.0
week 12: (50 + 80 + 120) / 3 = 83.3
Why: each result shares one odd value with its neighbours, so it is steadier but reacts late.
items.learnMore:
Smoothing with a window

A window of 3 averages the current value with the two before it. A longer window is smoother but slower to notice a real change; a shorter window reacts faster but lets more noise through.

Common mistake

Reading a moving average as if it were the current value. It lags, because older values are still inside the window.
items.reflection: Pick a number that bounces around for you, such as daily step counts or a weekly budget. What window length would let you see your direction without hiding a real change for too long?

items.prompt: Which change makes a 3-week moving average react faster to a lasting step up?
choices: A shorter window, at the cost of passing more noise through
A longer window, which gives recent values more weight
Extra earlier weeks, so that noise averages out faster
Sorting the window values from smallest to largest first
items.explanation: Fewer old values in the window means the new level takes over sooner, but less noise is averaged away.

items.prompt: The raw series rose 30 from week 10 (50) to week 11 (80), yet the 3-week average rose only 12.7. Why?
choices: Week 11 counts with weight one third and week 10 with two thirds
Week 11 enters while week 8 leaves, so it moves by (80 - 42) / 3
Moving averages rise by half of whatever the raw series rises
The average is over twelve weeks, so each week counts a twelfth
items.explanation: Sliding the window by one swaps the oldest value (42) for the newest (80), changing the sum by 38 and the average by 38 / 3 = 12.7.

items.prompt: Which line does least squares choose?
choices: The one through the first and the last point
The one through the largest value in the data
The one with the smallest total squared miss
items.explanation: Smallest sum of squared misses defines the fit.

items.prompt: Why square the misses?
choices: So the line must pass through every single point
So positive and negative misses cannot cancel
So the slope can never be negative in any case
items.explanation: Squares are never negative, and they also make large misses count more.

items.prompt: What does a miss of 3 contribute?
What does the slope mean?
choices: The value of y at the point where x is zero
The average of all of the y values together
Extra y for each one-step increase in x
items.explanation: Slope is the change per step.

items.prompt: What does the intercept mean?
choices: The change per step
Where the line sits at x = 0
The largest miss
items.explanation: It is the line's starting height.

items.prompt: A fitted slope of 4.34 for the bills means what?
choices: About $4.34 more per month along the line
The month-12 bill will be exactly $4.34 in total
The month-6 bill was $4.34 in total
items.explanation: Slope is dollars gained per month on the fitted line.

items.prompt: The line through all six bills gives which month-12 forecast?
Does least squares use only the last two points?
choices: Yes, the last two
No, it uses every point
Only the first and last
items.explanation: Every point contributes a miss to the total.

items.prompt: Line A misses three bills by 3, 3 and 3. Line B misses by 1, 1 and 7. Plain sums tie at 9. Which does least squares prefer?
choices: Line B: its two tiny misses count for more than the one big miss
Line A: squared totals are 27 and 51, so the big miss is punished
Neither: equal plain sums mean least squares cannot rank the lines
Line B: squaring makes the single largest miss count the least
items.explanation: 27 for A and 1 + 1 + 49 = 51 for B. Squaring makes one large miss cost more than several moderate ones.
items.reference:
Six bills, three lines
months 1-5 only: slope 0.50, month 12 = $56.10
all six months: slope 4.34, month 12 = $93.25
last jump extended: $28 a month, month 12 = $248
miss of 2 costs 4; miss of 10 costs 100
Why: squaring makes large misses expensive, so one late odd value tilts the line toward itself.
items.learnMore:
Fitting one line to every point

Least squares compares candidate lines by squaring each vertical miss and adding the squares; the smallest total wins. Squaring stops positive and negative misses cancelling and makes big misses count much more than small ones.

Common mistake

Believing the fitted line passes through the data. It balances all the misses, and usually touches few or none of the points.
items.reflection: Think of an estimate you make from many noisy readings, such as a typical travel time. Which single odd reading pulls your estimate most, and would you keep or drop it?

items.prompt: An equally odd bill appears in month 2 in one series and in month 6 in another. Which moves the month-12 forecast more?
choices: Month 2, because older values are always weighted more heavily
Equal, because squaring treats equal misses equally everywhere
Month 6, since the end of the range can tilt the line freely
Month 2, because the fitted line must start from that earlier point
items.explanation: A forecast extends the line past the end, so a late point rotates it with more effect. This extra pull is leverage.

The amount of rounding in the dollar figures
How many months were averaged
How much the single month-6 bill tilts the fitted line
items.explanation: The only difference between the fits is month 6, so the change in slope is its influence.

A flatter line, because it must average in the bill at month 0
A slope of 12, the average bill
A line through only month 1 and month 3
items.explanation: With zero misses available the best total is zero. Slope 2 and intercept 8 put month 4 at 16.

items.prompt: What is seasonality?
choices: A pattern that repeats at a fixed period
A one-off spike
A steady rise forever
items.explanation: The key feature is repetition on a schedule.

items.prompt: Which of these is seasonal?
choices: One storm in one month
A bill that rises $2 each month forever
Higher heating bills every winter
items.explanation: It repeats yearly; the storm is a one-off and the rise is trend.

items.prompt: How long is the cycle in a quarterly yearly pattern?
choices: Two quarters
Four quarters
Eight quarters
items.explanation: Four quarters make a year.

items.prompt: Quarter 9 is which quarter of the year?
choices: Q1
Q2
Q4
items.explanation: Quarters 1, 5 and 9 are all Q1s.

items.prompt: Quarter 9 should be compared with which earlier quarter?
choices: The previous Q3, quarter 7
The average of all quarters
The previous Q1, quarter 5
items.explanation: Compare like with like.

items.prompt: Yearly averages are 95 and 103. By how much did the trend rise?
choices: $2 a year
$8 a year
$198 a year

items.prompt: Q5 was $130 and the yearly growth is $8. Forecast for Q9?
What can a straight line do to seasonal data?
choices: Fit it perfectly every time
Make the seasons vanish from the data
Hide or even reverse the real trend
items.explanation: The seasonal tilt mixes into the slope.

items.prompt: The line through the eight quarterly bills has slope -0.38 though yearly averages rose 95 to 103. What caused this?
choices: The yearly averages are wrong because the quarters are unequal
Least squares ignores every second year of data in the series
The bills fell steadily and the yearly averages simply hide it
The repeating yearly pattern tilts the line and cancels the real rise
items.explanation: Within each cycle the seasonal values fall from Q1 to Q3, which tilts the line downward and offsets the $2-a-quarter rise.
items.reference:
Made-up quarterly bills
Q1-Q4: 122, 84, 76, 98 (average 95)
Q5-Q8: 130, 92, 84, 106 (average 103)
real trend: up $8 a year ($2 a quarter)
straight-line slope: -0.38, R squared 0.002
Why: a repeating pattern tilts the line, so compare the same position in each cycle, such as Q1 with Q1.
items.learnMore:
Patterns that repeat

Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at a fixed period, such as quarters or weekdays. A straight line averages that tilt in with the real trend, so compare each point with the same position in the previous cycle and then add the growth.

Common mistake

Fitting one line to two cycles and trusting the slope. The seasonal tilt can cancel the trend or even flip its sign.
items.reflection: Think of something in your life that peaks on a schedule, such as weekend spending or winter heating. What would a same-time-last-cycle comparison tell you that a plain recent average hides?

items.prompt: Q6 was $92 and yearly growth is $8. What is the same-quarter forecast for Q10?
items.explanation: Q10 is a Q2, so compare with Q6 and add the growth: 92 + 8 = 100.

This Saturday against last Saturday

The highest day against the lowest day

items.prompt: Which finding would most weaken "the month-6 spike was just summer"?

Last year's month 12 was higher than month 6
The same month the previous year had a normal bill
The bill arrives every month at a similar time
items.explanation: A seasonal cause should have repeated a year earlier. If it did not, summer is a weaker explanation.

items.prompt: R squared of 1 means what?
choices: The line explains none of the spread at all
The line passes through every point
The slope of the line is exactly equal to 1
items.explanation: No spread is left unexplained.

items.prompt: R squared near 0 means what?
choices: The line is no better than guessing the average
The fit is perfect and leaves nothing out
The forecast from the line is certain to be exact
items.explanation: ssRes is about as large as ssTot.

items.prompt: Which fit is better, R squared 0.944 or 0.606?
choices: They are equal
items.explanation: Higher means more of the spread is explained.

items.prompt: R squared 0.606 leaves about what share unexplained?
choices: About 61%
About 39%
About 6%

items.prompt: Which weeks does a straight line fit better?
choices: Weeks 1-10
Weeks 1-12
Weeks 11-12 on their own
items.explanation: The pre-viral weeks follow a gentle line closely.

items.prompt: What does ssTot measure?
choices: Distance of the values from the fitted line
The size of the slope of the fitted line
Spread of values around their overall average
items.explanation: It is the spread before any line is fitted.

items.prompt: What does ssRes measure?
choices: Total spread before fitting
The squared miss left after fitting
The intercept
items.explanation: It is the unexplained part.

items.prompt: Can R squared prove the next 40 weeks will follow the line?
choices: No, it only measures fit on the data used
Yes, a high value guarantees it
Yes, but only above 0.5
items.explanation: It is about the past data, not future behaviour.

items.prompt: A fit has R squared 0.944 on weeks 1-10. A colleague says the week-52 forecast is therefore 94% likely to be right. What is wrong?
choices: R squared must be at least 0.99 before any forecast may be made from a fitted line at all
R squared measures fit within the data used, not the chance a far forecast holds
The percentage should be subtracted from 100 before it is used here
R squared only ever applies to the first ten weeks of a series
items.explanation: Fit quality inside the observed range says nothing about whether the pattern survives forty more weeks.
items.reference:
Two fits of the signups
weeks 1-10: R squared 0.944, slope 2.04
weeks 1-12: R squared 0.606, slope 5.54
R squared = 1 - ssRes / ssTot
1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average
Why: R squared measures fit inside the fitted data; it does not promise the next forty weeks.
items.learnMore:
How much does the line explain?

ssTot is the spread of values around their overall average, and ssRes is the spread left around the fitted line. R squared is 1 - ssRes / ssTot, the share of the spread the line explains. It describes the data already seen.

Common mistake

Reading a high R squared as a probability that a forecast will come true. It only measures how well the line matches the points it was fitted to.
items.reflection: Think of a model or rule of thumb you rely on. What evidence do you have that it keeps working outside the situations that built your confidence in it?

items.prompt: Adding weeks 11-12 moved the slope from 2.04 to 5.54 and R squared from 0.944 to 0.606. Best reading?
choices: The slope rose from 2.04 to 5.54, so the new line must therefore describe the data better
The fit got worse only because there was more data in the series
Two edge points break the earlier pattern, tilting the line and worsening the fit
R squared always falls whenever any new points are added to a fit
items.explanation: The two viral weeks sit far from the early pattern, so the line tilts toward them and leaves more unexplained.

items.prompt: A series wiggles around 50 with no direction, and a fitted line has R squared near 0. Is that a bad fit?
choices: Yes, any fit near 0 means the data must be wrong somewhere
Yes, because the line ought to be forced through all the wiggles
No, because R squared near 0 always means a perfect fit
Not necessarily: a flat series gives a line little trend to explain
items.explanation: The best line is nearly flat, which equals the average, so it explains little variation because little is there to explain.

How much does the line explain?

ssTot is the spread of values around their overall average, and ssRes is the spread left around the fitted line. R squared is 1 - ssRes / ssTot, the share of the spread the line explains. It describes the data already seen.

Common mistake

Reading a high R squared as a probability that a forecast will come true. It only measures how well the line matches the points it was fitted to.
items.reflection: Think of a model or rule of thumb you rely on. What evidence do you have that it keeps working outside the situations that built your confidence in it?

items.prompt: For one fit, ssTot is 100 and ssRes is 25. What is R squared?
items.reference:
Two fits of the signups
weeks 1-10: R squared 0.944, slope 2.04
weeks 1-12: R squared 0.606, slope 5.54
R squared = 1 - ssRes / ssTot
1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average
Why: R squared measures fit inside the fitted data; it does not promise the next forty weeks.

items.prompt: Forecasting inside the observed range is called what?
choices: Extrapolation
Smoothing
Interpolation
items.explanation: Inside the range means interpolation; beyond it is extrapolation.

items.prompt: Which forecast is riskier, week 13 or week 52?
choices: Week 13
Week 52
They are equally risky
items.explanation: The further past the data, the more can change.

items.prompt: Does a straight line have a ceiling?
choices: No, it keeps rising or falling forever
Yes, it stops at the last observed value
Yes, it stops at twice the average value
items.explanation: A line has no built-in limit.

items.prompt: Two lines differ in slope. What happens to the gap at far weeks?
choices: It shrinks as the horizon gets longer
It stays exactly the same at every week
It grows with the horizon
items.explanation: The slope difference is multiplied by the week number.

items.prompt: The gap between the two signup fits at week 13 is?
A forecast quietly assumes what?
choices: That the pattern in the data continues
That noise in the data is exactly zero
That the very first point in the data was correct
items.explanation: Extrapolation continues what the data showed.

items.prompt: Which can end a trend?
choices: Only more data being collected
Nothing; trends never change
A ceiling, a competitor or a campaign ending
items.explanation: Real-world limits and events change trends.

items.prompt: How should a distant forecast be reported?
choices: As a single exact number
With its assumption and a range of alternatives
With no explanation at all
items.explanation: Distant forecasts are guesses, so say what they assume.

items.prompt: The gap between two fits grows by about 3.50 per week and was 30.8 at week 13. About how large is it at week 40?
choices: About 77
About 235
About 31
About 125
items.reference:
Gap between the 12-week and 10-week lines
week 13: 85.7 vs 54.9, gap 30.8
week 30: 179.8 vs 89.5, gap 90.3
week 52: 301.7 vs 134.3, gap 167.4
gap = (5.54 - 2.04) x week - 14.73
Why: a difference in slope is multiplied by the horizon, so distant forecasts disagree most.
items.learnMore:
Horizon and what a line cannot see

A forecast is slope times the week number plus the intercept, so any slope error grows linearly with how far out you project. A straight line also cannot see a ceiling, a campaign ending, or a change of season.

Common mistake

Reporting one exact number for a distant week. Report the assumption and a range of plausible alternatives.
items.reflection: Think of a plan you made far ahead based on a recent trend. What change could have broken that trend, and how would you have noticed it early?

items.prompt: Assume, for illustration, the reachable audience caps at about 150 signups a week. Which statement holds?
choices: 302 is impossible under the cap, and 134 may be wrong if growth stops sooner
Both are fine, because straight lines never exceed any such cap
Only 1,720 is excluded; 302 is still reachable by week 52
302 is certain, because the line fits the observed data so well
items.explanation: The line has no ceiling, so it can predict values the cap forbids. Even a forecast under the cap assumes growth continues until then.

items.prompt: Which forecast is the safest to make with a straight line?
choices: Bills ten years out when a new heating system is planned
Next month's bill when two years show a steady rise
Signups a year after a viral post, extended in a line
A yearly cycle forecast from one quarter
items.explanation: Short horizon, long stable history, no known change: nothing here breaks the straight-line assumption.

items.prompt: Two reasonable fits disagree widely at a far week. Best response?
choices: Pick the larger forecast so the plan is not short
Average the two and present it as exact
Report a range and name the assumption behind each line
Refit using only the final week so there is one answer
items.explanation: Disagreement between sensible fits is itself the measure of uncertainty. Hiding it does not remove it.

items.prompt: Implement `mean(xs)`: the average of an array of numbers.
items.explanation: Add the values and divide by how many there are.

items.prompt: Implement `predict(slope, intercept, x)`: the value of the line at x.
items.explanation: The line is slope times x plus intercept; at x = 0 only the intercept remains.

items.prompt: Implement `miss(actual, predicted)`: how far the actual value is above the prediction (negative if below).
items.explanation: A miss is actual minus predicted, so sign shows the direction.

items.prompt: Implement `squaredMiss(actual, predicted)`: the squared miss.
items.explanation: Squaring removes the sign and punishes large misses.

items.prompt: Implement `totalSquaredMiss(xs, ys, slope, intercept)`: the sum of squared misses between each y and the line.
items.explanation: This is the quantity least squares minimizes: add up each point's squared miss from the line.

items.prompt: Implement `lastThreeAverage(values)`: the mean of the last three values of an array of at least three numbers.
items.explanation: Take the final window of three values and average it.

items.prompt: Implement `twoPointSlope(x1, y1, x2, y2)`: the slope of the line through two points.
items.explanation: Rise over run. This is exactly the naive two-point trend.

items.prompt: Implement `naiveForecast(last, previous, steps)`: the last value plus the last change repeated for the given number of steps.
items.explanation: The change is last minus previous; repeating it adds steps copies to the last value.

items.prompt: Implement `fitLine(xs, ys)` returning `{ slope, intercept }` by least squares: slope is the sum of (x - xMean)(y - yMean) divided by the sum of (x - xMean) squared, and intercept is yMean - slope * xMean.
items.explanation: The slope compares how x and y move together with how spread out x is. The intercept makes the line pass through the point of averages.
items.reference:
Fitting a line is four sums
average x and average y
num = sum of (x - xMean) x (y - yMean)
den = sum of (x - xMean) squared
slope = num / den; intercept = yMean - slope x xMean
Why: writing the sums out shows exactly why every point, not just the last two, shapes the slope.
items.learnMore:
Computing the fit

The slope compares how x and y move together (num) with how spread out x is (den). Because every point adds to both sums, the slope is shaped by all of them, and the line always passes through the point of averages.

Common mistake

Forgetting to subtract the averages, or dividing by the number of points instead of by den. Both give a slope that is silently wrong.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you use that is really a weighted summary of many past cases. Which cases carry the most weight in it, and is that deliberate?

items.prompt: Implement `forecastAt(xs, ys, x)`: fit the least-squares line to the points and return its value at x.
items.explanation: Fit first, then plug the future x into slope times x plus intercept. A constant series has slope 0, so it forecasts the same value forever.

items.prompt: Implement `rSquared(xs, ys, slope, intercept)`: 1 minus ssRes divided by ssTot, where ssRes is the sum of squared misses from the line and ssTot is the sum of squared distances of y from its mean.
items.explanation: ssTot is the spread before fitting and ssRes is what the line leaves behind. A perfect line leaves nothing (1), and a line at the mean leaves everything (0).
